## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

B. Cowell's translation as the tale of "Luckie and Blackie", is a narrative of the Bodhisatta's past life set at the Bamboo Grove near Rājagaha concerning Devadatta [Braarvig]. In this past birth, the Bodhisatta was a chief stag who instructed his two sons in the art of herd leadership; one son (identified with Sāriputta) adhered to his father's advice and successfully led his herd to safety and prosperity, while the other son (identified with Devadatta) rejected his counsel and brought his herd to ruin [Nyanaponika et al. 2003]. The narrative exemplifies a regular pattern across the Jātaka collection illustrating the moral and practical dichotomies of wisdom versus foolishness and virtue versus wickedness in the past relationship between the Buddha's chief disciples and Devadatta [Braarvig].

- [DharmaNexus] DharmaNexus text reuse and alignment database — Confirmed absence of Pali-internal text reuse or significant cross-language alignments.
- [Braarvig] Jens Braarvig, The Buddhist Hell — Noted Cowell's alternative title 'Luckie and Blackie' and the story's function in contrasting wise and foolish past lives of Devadatta.
- [Nyanaponika et al. 2003] Nyanaponika Thera, Hellmuth Hecker, and Bhikkhu Bodhi, Great Disciples of the Buddha: Their Lives, Their Works, Their Legacy (2003) — Provided the plot summary: the Bodhisatta as a chief stag instructing his two sons, identified as Sāriputta and Devadatta.
